text: On December 7, 1941, Japanese fighter planes attacked Pearl Harbor, striking the U.S. Pacific Fleet and killing over 2,400 people. For years, the United States had stood apart from the war tearing through Europe, refusing to support its allies as fascism spread across continents. But the moment bombs fell on American soil, neutrality vanished. The war was no longer foreign. It was personal and urgent. Within months, the U.S. mobilized not just its own territory, but Canada’s North. Engineers and soldiers crossed into Sahtú Dene land to launch the Canol Project: a massive, hastily planned wartime pipeline across Indigenous territory. The Canol Project, short for Canadian Oil, was a massive U.S.-led wartime infrastructure operation launched in 1942. It involved the construction of a 600-kilometre pipeline from Norman Wells, Northwest Territories to a newly built refinery in Whitehorse, Yukon, along with a road, pump stations, telegraph lines, and airfields. Designed to supply fuel for Allied military operations in Alaska during World War II, the project was completed at breakneck speed under harsh subarctic conditions. It cost over $130 million USD, operated for just 13 months, and was abandoned in 1945, leaving behind widespread environmental damage and a legacy of disruption on Sahtú Dene and Métis lands. Canol Pipeline from Norman Wells to the NWT - Yukon border US Military Dodge CW Utility Vehicle in Devil’s Pass - Mile 110 It was sold as a defensive necessity, designed to protect Alaska and supply oil for Allied forces. But for the Sahtú Dene and Métis, it was something else entirely: a foreign occupation launched without warning, consent, or respect. Allies, Except at Home: How the U.S. Entered Sahtú Lands Without Consent By 1941, Canada was already deep in the fight against Nazi Germany. As a Dominion of the British Empire, it had declared war on Germany in 1939, two years before the United States, and had already suffered losses in Europe and Hong Kong. Canadian soldiers were dying alongside British and French forces while America watched from the sidelines, hesitant to get involved in a “foreign war.” That changed abruptly on December 7, 1941, when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. With its Pacific fleet crippled and Alaska suddenly exposed, the United States panicked. The war was now not just a distant obligation, it was on their doorstep. And they needed oil. Canada’s North, particularly the Norman Wells oilfield, became strategically critical. To feed the war machine, the U.S. scrambled to build a secure, continental supply chain: pipelines, refineries, roads, and airstrips, projects like the Alaska Highway and the Canol Project. But there was a problem: these plans extended deep into Canadian territory, including the Sahtú Dene and Métis territories that Canada occupied. The Permission That Was and Wasn’t Granted In early 1942, diplomatic negotiations between Ottawa and Washington moved swiftly. Canada, under Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King, agreed to allow U.S. military forces and contractors to operate on Canadian soil to support the war effort. These permissions were granted quietly, under the logic of shared Allied defense, and often in informal or secretive agreements rather than transparent treaties. The Canol Project was approved under this broader umbrella with the understanding that the U.S. would build the pipeline, refinery, and road, then hand them over to Canada once the war ended. But while Ottawa and Washington exchanged notes and signed off on logistics, no one consulted the people whose land would be most directly affected. The Sahtú Dene and Métis were never asked. No treaty was negotiated. No consent was sought. No compensation was offered. “We weren’t told about any agreement. The government in Ottawa didn’t ask us, and the Americans didn’t care. They just came.” — Elder from Tulita, fictionalized from oral history accounts To the federal government, the Northwest Territories were a remote, sparsely populated frontier; administered, but not protected. The colonial view saw Indigenous land as unoccupied and unentitled. So when American bulldozers tore through traplines, rivers, and ancestral trails, it wasn’t seen as a violation, it was seen as progress. “Canada said yes on our behalf. But we never said yes. That’s not partnership. That’s dispossession.” — Sahtú youth leader, paraphrased from community consultation sessions The diplomatic permissions granted to the U.S. may have had strategic logic in the halls of Ottawa and Washington. But on the ground in the Sahtú, they looked and felt like something else entirely: a land invasion, dressed in Allied flags. “We Were Just in the Way”: The Sahtú Dene and the Canol Invasion Before the bulldozers came, the Sahtú Dene and Métis lived along the Mackenzie River as they had for generations, hunting moose and caribou, trapping in winter, gathering medicines and berries, and moving with the rhythms of the land. Their knowledge of the land was intimate, built over thousands of years. The river was their highway, the forest their storehouse, the mountains their sanctuary. Mackenzie River near Norman Wells, NWT Carcajou River at the entrance to Dodo Canyon looking east towards the Mackenzie River Then came the war. In the winter of 1942–43, without warning or consultation, thousands of U.S. Army personnel and civilian contractors arrived in the Sahtú region. They came with tanks, trucks, sawmills, cranes, and a timetable dictated not by the land, but by the Pentagon. In just months, the quiet muskeg trails and game-rich valleys were gouged open for a road and pipeline that the locals had neither asked for nor agreed to. The Sahtú Dene watched their traplines bulldozed, their cabins burned or appropriated, and their trails swallowed by the mud churned up by heavy equipment. Some tried to speak to the American soldiers, but were met with indifference or misunderstanding. Others were hired as guides, laborers, or hunters, paid in canned food, tobacco, or wages that rarely matched the value of the knowledge they provided. Many elders remember the Canol Project as a time of chaos and disruption. In oral histories collected decades later, Sahtú Dene spoke of game animals fleeing the noise, of fish poisoned by oil spills, and of being treated as invisible on their own land. One elder, recalling the project, said: “They never asked. They just came and built everything. We were just in the way.” The trauma was not only environmental. The arrival of outside workers brought disease, alcohol, and new forms of dependency. Families were displaced, traditions interrupted, and social bonds tested by the sudden pressure of war-driven industrialization. For the Sahtú Dene, the Canol Project was not just a pipeline, it was an invasion. A foreshadowing of what development would mean for Indigenous peoples across the North: uninvited, disruptive, and dirty. A Toxic Legacy: What the Canol Project Left Behind The rusting skeleton of World War II ambition still scars the landscape to this day. What remains today is one of North America’s longest and most remote trails. But far from being just a wartime relic, the Canol Trail is a living reminder of colonial disregard—for Indigenous peoples, for ecosystems, and for the land itself. Rusted vehicles and equipment abandoned along the pipeline Fuel drums and waste abandoned in the alpine The project cut through Sahtú Dene and Métis land without consultation or consent. It disrupted wildlife migration routes, desecrated sacred landscapes, and left behind a toxic legacy that is still being cleaned up decades later. When the Canol pipeline shut down in 1945, barely a year after it began operating, it left a toxic footprint that has taken generations to fully understand, let alone address. Even during its short operation, the Canol pipeline leaked repeatedly, due to rushed construction, poor welding, and the brutal conditions of the North. Crude oil and fuel spills contaminated snowpack, rivers, and ground. The pipeline broke down over 80 times in just 13 months, according to post-war assessments. Emergency repairs often involved simply rerouting the flow around broken sections, leaving spills to soak into the muskeg and taiga. But the real damage came after the war. Thousands of drums of oil and fuel were abandoned along the route. Some leaked over time, their contents seeping into the soil. Vehicles, generators, and fuel tanks were left to rust and rupture. Old batteries oozed lead and acid. And hundreds of wooden buildings, many insulated with asbestos, were left to decay in place, slowly releasing hazardous fibres into the air and ground. The most dangerous sites included: Norman Wells, where industrial operations contaminated soil and groundwater; Camp Canol, near the Mackenzie River, where the remains of a U.S. military base included oil-soaked soils, PCBs, lead-based paints, and asbestos debris; and The pipeline route itself, littered with corroding pipe, ruptured drums, and collapsing bridges. Pump Station #2 near Mile 36 Pipes entering Pump Station #2 near Mile 36 Relic US military vehicle at Devil’s Pass Rusted vehicles abandoned at a road maintenance camp near Mile 80 The physical remains of the Canol Project are scattered across Sahtú territory, but its deepest legacy is felt in the lives and memories of the people who live there. For many, the rusting debris and poisoned soil are reminders of a time when their land and lives were treated as expendable. “They came and went like a storm. We were left with nothing but garbage and sickness.” — Elder from Tulita, quoted in a Canol Trail oral history project “I remember playing near those old buildings when I was a kid. We didn’t know it was asbestos. No one warned us. Our parents didn’t even know what it was.” — Community member, Norman Wells “It’s our land. We should have been the first to be asked, not the last to be told.” — Young Dene environmental worker, Fort Good Hope The environmental damage is also tied to cultural loss. Many Sahtú Dene describe how contamination disrupted not just the ecology, but the continuity of their way of life. “There are places my grandfather used to trap that we can’t go anymore. There’s oil in the water, and animals avoid it. It’s not just the land that was damaged, it’s our stories, our teachings.” — Sahtú Dene trapper, Tulita For decades, the contamination went unacknowledged and unremediated, despite ongoing concerns from Sahtú communities. Children played in abandoned buildings filled with friable asbestos. Hunters encountered oil drums in creek beds. Elders warned about fish and wildlife near certain sites. These voices remind us that the Canol Trail is not just a remote hiking route or forgotten wartime project. For the Sahtú Dene, it is an open wound, but also a site of resilience, where a new generation is reclaiming control over how their land is restored, remembered, and respected. Cleanup and Control: Reclaiming the Canol For decades after the Canol Project was abandoned, the Canadian and U.S. governments largely ignored the mess left behind. The Sahtú Dene, who lived with the consequences, were left to watch the land they depended on quietly degrade, its waters tainted, its soil blackened, its hunting and trapping trails blocked by wreckage. That began to change in the 1990s. Growing public concern about environmental contamination in the North, alongside persistent pressure from Dene leaders, finally forced the federal government to act. Sahtú Dene advocacy was the turning point, reframing the Canol not just as a wartime artifact but as a long-standing environmental injustice. In the early 2000s, INAC (now Indigenous Services Canada) launched a series of remediation efforts focused on the most contaminated sites, starting with Camp Canol, one of the largest and most toxic hotspots. Cleanup involved: Asbestos removal from collapsing buildings; Excavation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil; Removal and disposal of hazardous materials like lead-acid batteries, PCBs, and rusted fuel drums; and Stabilization of eroded areas and waste piles. The cleanup has brought some hope, but also reopened wounds. Community members recall the frustration of being sidelined during the project’s construction, and again during early discussions of remediation. Even among those now working on cleanup crews or monitoring teams, the sense of injustice lingers. “They left us the mess, but now we’re cleaning it up. At least now our kids can be part of fixing it. That matters.” — Dene youth technician, Canol Trail remediation project Some of this work is now complete, but remediation is an ongoing process. The terrain is remote and expensive to access. There are still dozens of small contaminated sites scattered along the trail and pipeline corridor. Many are on or near culturally important lands, areas where Dene families have camped, hunted, or gathered medicines for generations. Sahtú Dene Leadership in Land Restoration Today, the Sahtú Dene are not just observers, they are leaders in the cleanup and future stewardship of the trail. Under the Sahtú Dene and Métis Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement, signed in 1993, the people of the region have formal co-management authority over their lands. As a result, they are actively involved in decision-making about cleanup priorities, environmental monitoring, and future land use. Recovering scars of the pipeline in the Mackenzie Valley floodplain Local Indigenous-owned companies have been contracted for remediation work, environmental assessments, and helicopter transport. Dene youth are being trained in land stewardship, sampling, and restoration techniques, blending traditional knowledge with scientific methods. The vision is not just to clean the land, but to reconnect people to it. There is also a growing conversation about transforming the Canol Trail into a territorial park, led by the Sahtú Renewable Resources Board and community governments. But for many Dene, this can’t happen unless the site is properly cleaned, sacred areas protected, and their role as stewards made central, not symbolic. The Canol cleanup is far from over. But it marks a shift: from military occupation to restoring stolen Indigenous stewardship. From neglect to responsibility. From a story of erasure to one of resurgence. Looking Forward: From Ruin to Responsibility The story of the Canol Trail is not just about a failed pipeline. It is about who bears the burden when governments and industries make decisions without consent. It is about the slow violence of contamination, and the long memory of the land. It is about the people who are still living with that legacy, and working to heal from it. As we confront today’s infrastructure debates - pipelines, roads, mines, and energy corridors - we have to ask: what has really changed? Are we still building in the name of national interest while ignoring the cost to Indigenous nations? Or are we finally learning to listen, to share power, and to plan for futures that do not leave people and ecosystems behind? The Sahtú Dene never asked for a pipeline. But now, through cleanup and co-management, they are shaping what happens next. Their work to restore the Canol Trail is not just cleanup, it’s reclamation. Of land. Of sovereignty. Of voice. In an age of infrastructure urgency and reconciliation rhetoric, the Canol Trail stands as both a warning and an invitation. Can we build urgently needed infrastructure projects while ensuring both consent from, and long term benefit for the affected nations? Photo Credits: Kyle Hunt Thanks for reading! The Canadian Pacific Railway, completed in 1885, is often mythologized as the steel thread that stitched together a fragile Confederation. Politicians claimed it was the only way to bind British Columbia to the rest of Canada. Businessmen saw profit. Settlers saw opportunity. The state saw a tool for sovereignty. But beneath the patriotic narratives lies a darker truth; one of dislocation, environmental upheaval, and broken promises to Indigenous peoples. Last Breath of the Buffalo It was 1879, and the sun hung low over the shortgrass prairie near what is now Medicine Hat, Alberta. The wind curled through the coulees, carrying no sound; no hoofbeats, no snorts, no thunder of life. The great herds were gone. Just a decade earlier, this land had shaken under the weight of tens of thousands of buffalo, moving like a dark wave across the earth. The Plains Cree, who had followed the herds for generations, knew these rhythms as intimately as breath and heartbeat. But now the land was silent, scraped clean by men who came with rifles, trains, and hunger for empire. Downwind, just beyond the coulee ridge, a group of European-American hunters moved methodically. They were from Montana, but had pushed north into Canadian territory with the promise of easy kills. Their camp smelled of gun oil, grease, and sun-rotted hide. Buffalo robes were stacked like cordwood, thick with flies. They were not hunting for food. They were hunting for extinction. Each man carried a .50-calibre Sharps rifle, the infamous “buffalo gun.” From 800 yards out, the weapon could split a beast’s spine. Spot a herd, shoot the leaders, and wait. A good team could kill a hundred buffalo in a day. They would take only the hides, perhaps the tongues, and leave the rest to rot. The stench of it blew eastward, toward a Cree winter camp near the South Saskatchewan River. Women boiled bark and moss. Children cried through the night. Elders told stories of days when the earth moved with life. Hunters returned with nothing but dry feet and bitter news. In government dispatches, the news was cold and calculated. Indian Commissioner Edgar Dewdney kept food stores locked in Fort Walsh, rationing them only to chiefs who agreed to Treaty 6. 'Give them nothing until they are on the verge of starving,' one bureaucrat advised. 'Then they will sign.' In the U.S., General Sheridan was more blunt: 'Kill every buffalo you can. Every buffalo dead is an Indian gone.' That night, a Cree hunter watched the red sky sink. He had not fired his musket in days. His horse was bone-thin. He saw vultures circling the settler kill site, picking flesh from torn carcasses. The meat, once sacred, now left to spoil. A boy asked him when the buffalo would return. He did not answer. A Manufactured Collapse The extermination of the North American plains bison (buffalo) in the 19th century was not an ecological accident, it was an intentional act, one that had devastating consequences for the Plains Cree, Blackfoot and Assiniboine. The extermination of buffalo severed the foundations of their economies, cultures, and sovereignties, and paved the way for the Canadian Pacific Railway expansion and settler colonization. In the early 1800s, buffalo herds on the plains numbered 30–60 million. By the 1880s, they were virtually extinct in Canada, with fewer than 500 animals remaining in the wild. Colonial officials encouraged buffalo extermination to starve Indigenous populations into submission. The Canadian government allowed the collapse of the herds to facilitate treaty signings and land surrender. As the buffalo disappeared in the 1870s and 1880s, the Plains Cree entered a period of crisis. Without buffalo, they faced starvation, disease, and coercion from the government, which withheld food rations to force treaty signings. "We were rich, my people, but you took away our richness. We had plenty of buffalo, plenty of everything. But now we are poor." — Chief Big Bear, 1885 trial statement "We do not want to sign away our land. We want the government to listen to us as a people. We want to live as we did before, following the buffalo and praying to the spirits." — Attributed to a Cree speaker, Treaty 6 discussions, Fort Pitt, 1876. Tracks of Displacement The construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was not simply a technical or economic project, it was a deliberate act of colonization. To make way for the tracks, the Canadian government needed to secure control over vast swaths of Indigenous land. This meant removing the original inhabitants through a combination of coercive treaties, forced relocation, and legal restrictions on Indigenous mobility and resistance. Massive land acquisitions were secured through treaties that were often signed under pressure, misunderstood, or outright violated. In British Columbia, most of the land the railway traversed was never ceded at all. In the Prairies, the Crown rushed to sign treaties (like Treaties 1–7) before track-laying began, aiming not at fair agreements but at clearing Indigenous people from land for settlers and rail access. The Indian Act (1876) and the aggressive enforcement of the pass system helped prevent Indigenous resistance, ensuring people could not move freely near the rail lines, even on their own traditional territories. In the 1870s and 1880s, just as plans for the Canadian Pacific Railway were solidifying, the federal government rushed to negotiate Treaties 1 through 7, covering most of what is now Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. These treaties were ostensibly peaceful agreements between the Crown and Indigenous Nations, including the Anishinaabe, Cree, Assiniboine, and Blackfoot Confederacy. In reality, many were signed under duress and deception: Treaty 6 (1876) was signed by the Plains and Woods Cree in parts of central Alberta and Saskatchewan. Chief Mistahimaskwa (Big Bear) of the Plains Cree initially refused to sign, stating that the terms were insufficient and likening the forced settlement onto reserves to "pulling a rope around a person’s neck, denying them freedom on their land." However, facing starvation due to the collapse of the bison population, Big Bear was compelled to sign an adhesion to the treaty in 1882. This was not negotiation, it was coercion through hunger. Treaty 7 (1877) was signed at Blackfoot Crossing by the Blackfoot Confederacy (Siksika, Kainai, Piikani), the Nakoda (Stoney), and the Tsuut’ina nations. Their leaders believed they were agreeing to share the land, not surrender it entirely. Chief Crowfoot of the Siksika Nation reportedly said, "The Queen's men said we would always sit on softest feathers," reflecting the belief that the treaty would ensure their well-being. Crucially, the treaty was signed after surveyors and railway scouts had already begun mapping routes, the deal was a formality to justify what had already begun. Meanwhile, in British Columbia, where the Canadian Pacific Railway would eventually reach the Pacific, no treaties were signed at all across the vast majority of the territory. The tracks crossed through unceded territories of nations like the Secwépemc, Nlaka’pamux, Stó:lō, Tsilhqot’in, and many others, whose rights were simply ignored by colonial governments. Once land was secured, or presumed to be, the state turned to control and containment of Indigenous peoples. The Indian Act of 1876 created a legal framework that redefined Indigenous nations as wards of the state. One of the most oppressive tools developed under this framework was the pass system. Though never codified in law, the pass system was widely enforced from the 1880s through the 1940s, particularly on the Prairies. Under this system, Indigenous people living on reserves were required to obtain a written pass from an Indian agent to leave their community. No pass? You could be detained or forcibly returned to your reserve. This was a direct response to growing Indigenous resistance, including the 1885 Northwest Resistance led by Louis Riel and supported by Cree and Métis allies. The Canadian state feared further uprisings, especially along the vulnerable railway corridor, so it used the pass system to isolate communities, suppress political organization, and disrupt cultural continuity. Indian agents, backed by the North-West Mounted Police (now RCMP), monitored railway routes and enforced movement restrictions. In many areas, Indigenous people were forbidden from crossing rail lines, even when the tracks ran through their own territories. This ensured the CPR remained secure, and kept Indigenous presence out of settler sightlines. The combined effect of these policies was profound: entire nations were dispossessed, starved into submission, and confined. Lands that had been stewarded for millennia were turned into survey grids, towns, and rail sidings, without consent and without compensation. Today, the echoes of that displacement still reverberate. Many Indigenous communities along the railway continue to face poverty, environmental degradation, and limited land rights, even as Canadian Pacific Kansas City (formerly Canadian Pacific Railway) profits from routes laid atop their ancestors’ lands. First Nation communities along the line face dangerous rail crossings, no profit-sharing, and no say in how the lines are maintained or expanded, while the rail company has profited massively from land granted in the 19th century, land that in many cases was never the Crown’s to give. A Country Worth Connecting This story of buffalo bones and steel rails is not just history, it is the foundation beneath every pipeline, highway, transmission line, and railway that follows. The Canadian Pacific Railway didn’t just connect a country; it dispossessed nations, and built wealth on the ashes of economies it helped destroy. As Canada faces a new era of infrastructure expansion, for energy corridors, critical minerals, green transportation, and climate adaptation, the question is no longer just what we build, but how and with whom. True reconciliation demands more than land acknowledgments or one-off consultations. It requires structural shifts in how infrastructure is financed, governed, and owned; decision-making power that sits with Indigenous governments, not above them; equity partnerships where First Nations are not stakeholders, but rights-holders and co-owners; and projects must deliver long-term generational benefit, not just short-term mitigation. There are examples emerging: Indigenous-led transmission projects in Ontario and Manitoba, majority-First-Nation ownership of pipelines in Alberta, and co-developed and co-owned clean energy ventures in the North. These are not just reconciliatory gestures, they are models of economic justice, environmental stewardship, and political renewal. But the legacy of the Canadian Pacific Railway reminds us what happens when infrastructure is used to erase, rather than include. The story we tell about the past shapes what we imagine for the future. The rail line united Canada, yes, but it also divided Nations, lands, lives, and laws in ways that echo into the present. If Canada is to build again, it must do so not on the backs of Indigenous Nations, but in full partnership with them. That is how we make the land whole again. That is how we make a country worth connecting. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Lake in September In September, Lake Huron turns the colour of hammered copper in the late afternoon. The wind comes off the water cold and smells of fish and distance. If you grew up on that shore, you know that smell the way you know your own hands. Clifford George grew up on Stoney Point. His family had been there as long as anyone could remember, fishing the lake, trapping along the creek corridors, burying their dead in the sandy ground above the shoreline. The Anishinabbe name for the place was Aazhoodena. It meant something like “the other village,” the quieter settlement of the Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, separated from the main reserve by a few kilometres of boreal edge and farmland. In the spring of 1942, men in suits came to the band office with maps and a piece of paper. They were at war, they said. Canada needed the land for a training camp. It would be temporary, they said. The government would pay $15 per acre. And when the war was over, the land would return. The families of Aazhoodena were given thirty days to pack and leave. Clifford George’s family moved to Kettle Point, the main reserve. They took what they could carry. They left the rest, the gardens, the traplines, the graves. They left the graves. The war ended in 1945, but the. The land was not returned did not come back. It was not returned, and did not come back in 1950, 1960, or 1970. The Canadian military continued to run summer cadet training on the base through the 1990s. The burial grounds sat beneath the parade square and the vehicle yard. The families of Aazhoodena waited, wrote letters, filed requests, hired lawyers, and were ignored for fifty years. By 1993, some of them had stopped waiting. They moved back to the land. Dudley George was one of them. He was 38 years old in the summer of 1995. He was known in the community as a gentle, funny man, the kind of person who made people laugh. He was not a politician or a lawyer. He was someone who believed, that the land was theirs, and that fifty years was long enough to wait. On the night of September 6, 1995, Dudley George walked out of Ipperwash Provincial Park carrying a stick. An OPP sniper named Ken Deane fired three shots. George was hit and badly wounded. His sister Carolyn and brother Pierre loaded him into a car and tried to drive to the hospital. The police stopped them and held them for over an hour. Dudley George was declared dead at Strathroy Hospital on September 7, 1995. He was the first Indigenous person shot to death by police in Canada in over a century. What the Government Took, and Why The Stoney Point Reserve along the Lake Huron shoreline had stood for generations before 1942. It was a tiny fraction of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stoney Point’s Chippewas of Kettle and Stoney Point’s traditional territory that was taken by the British Crown through the coercive numbered treaty process of the 19th century (Treaty 29). The further expropriation in 1942that year happened under the War Measures Act, the same legislation that would later be used to intern Japanese Canadians and, a generation later, to suspend civil liberties during the FLQ crisis. It was a blunt instrument, designed for emergencies, with no requirement for negotiation or consent. The government offered fifteen dollars an acre, a price the band rejected. The government took the land anyway. Thirty-one families were relocated. Homes were moved or bulldozed—the military erected fences around the burial ground. The base was named Camp Ipperwash. The promise to return the land was informal, the kind of assurance that sounds reasonable in wartime and disappears into bureaucratic fog once the shooting stops. There was no binding legal commitment, no sunset clause, no reversion mechanism in the expropriation order. And so when the war ended, and federal priorities shifted, the land simply stayed federal. Year after year, through Liberal and Conservative governments alike, requests to honour the original commitment were acknowledged and shelved. By the 1980s, the Stoney Point people had made the issue a formal political demand. By 1993, a group of them, Clifford George among them, had moved onto the base itself. In July 1995, they occupied the barracks and evicted the military. The cadets left. The Stoney Pointers stayed. Then, on Labour Day weekend, a group of about 35 community members, including women and teenage boys, occupied the adjacent Ipperwash Provincial Park. They had waited until the seasonal campers had gone. They came peacefully to draw attention to the burial ground within the park boundary and to the decades-old land claim that no government had seen fit to resolve. What happened next says a great deal about who Ontario thought it was in 1995, and who it thought the Stoney Point people were. “I Want the Fucking Indians Out of the Park” On September 5, the day after the park occupation began, Premier Mike Harris convened a meeting of senior Ontario officials, including the Solicitor General and senior staff. The meeting was held at the Premier’s office at Queen’s Park. The notes from that meeting record its conclusion plainly: the province would take steps to remove the occupiers as soon as possible. Former Attorney General Charles Harnick testified at the Ipperwash Inquiry years later that Premier Harris had said, at that meeting: “I want the fuck—ing Indians out of the park.” Harris denied making the statement. Justice Sidney B. Linden, who chaired the inquiry, found that Harris had likely said it, though he concluded the comment had limited direct effect on the OPP’s tactical decisions that night. That conclusion has been debated. What is not debated is that within hours of the Queen’s Park meeting, the OPP began mobilizing a tactical response, including the deployment of the Tactics and Rescue Unit, the force’s elite tactical team, to Ipperwash. The OPP also received intelligence from CSIS, Canada’s domestic spy agency, that there were weapons on the base. Documents declassified and reported on in 2025 show that CSIS had been actively investigating what it internally called “Native extremism” at Ipperwash in the weeks before the shooting. The characterization is striking. These were people trying to reclaim land their families had been evicted from by force. Land that represented a tiny fraction of their Traditional Territory already taken by the Crown. , landLand with a promise attached to it, land containing their ancestors’ graves. CSIS saw terrorism. Justice Linden later found the protesters had no guns. They had bats, sticks, and stones. On the night of September 6, the OPP staged a nighttime confrontation near the park entrance. A car and a school bus moved out of the park. Acting Sergeant Ken Deane, positioned with a four-man sharpshooter team, fired at Dudley George. His defence, at trial, was that George had been carrying a rifle. The judge rejected that claim outright, finding that Deane had invented it to conceal the fact that he had shot an unarmed man. Deane was convicted of criminal negligence causing death. He received a conditional sentence of two years less a day, to be served in the community, plus 180 hours of community service. He did not serve a single day in prison. He was later ordered to resign from the OPP. He died in a car accident in February 2006, while awaiting his turn to testify at the Ipperwash Inquiry. For eight years after the shooting, under the Harris government, there was no official inquiry. The George family and their lawyers pushed for one. Human rights organizations called for one. The answer, every time, was no. When Dalton McGuinty’s Liberals came to power in 2003, they launched the inquiry almost immediately. Justice Linden’s final report was delivered in May 2007. The Inquiry, the Findings, and What They Mean The Ipperwash Inquiry heard four years of testimony. It examined the political interference leading up to the shooting, the OPP’s tactical choices, the behaviour of individual officers, and the broader systemic failures that produced the crisis. Justice Linden’s findings were unsparing. He found that some OPP officers had been ignorant of Indigenous history and the legal context of the protest. He found that others held explicitly racist views, describing Indigenous people in terms the inquiry report would not repeat. He found that the rush to remove the occupiers, driven at least in part by political pressure from Queen’s Park, had compressed the timeline in ways that preempted foreclosed non-violent options. He also found something larger: that Ipperwash was not an isolated incident. It was the product of a relationship between the Crown and Indigenous peoples in Ontario that was broken at its foundations. The inquiry recommended that the province return Ipperwash Provincial Park to the Kettle and Stony Point First Nation. It called for improved police training on Indigenous rights and history. It called for a formal First Nations consultation process before police deployments related to Indigenous occupations. It recommended changes to how Ontario handled longstanding land disputes, so that communities would not have to occupy land to get the government’s attention. It did not recommend criminal charges against Mike Harris. The question of whether the premier’s statement had legally caused the shooting was, Linden found, too attenuated to establish. What the inquiry could not do was place Ipperwash within the broader legal framework taking shape in Canadian courts at the time. That work was happening elsewhere. In 1997, the Supreme Court of Canada decided Delgamuukw v British Columbia, recognizing that Aboriginal title was a real and enforceable interest in land, not merely a historical claim to be managed by the Crown. In 2004, Haida Nation v British Columbia established that the duty to consult arose before any Crown decision that could adversely affect Aboriginal rights, even before those rights were proven in court. Together, these decisions were reshaping what governments were legally required to do before acting on Indigenous lands. Ipperwash sits awkwardly in this legal arc. The Anishinabbe of Kettle and Stoney Point people were not arguing Aboriginal title. They were arguing something more basic: that the federal government had made a promise, taken their land under wartime emergency powers, and then broken that promise for fifty years. No consultation framework, no matter how well designed, addresses what to do when the Crown simply refuses to follow through on a commitment it made in 1942. What Haida Nation and the cases that followed it do establish is that the kind of political short-circuit that happened at Ipperwash — (i.e. a premier deciding at a meeting that protesters need to be removed, with police deployed the same night, without any genuine engagement with the underlying land rights issue) — is exactly what the duty to consult is designed to prevent. The Crown cannot run out the clock on Indigenous rights by ignoring them until the situation becomes acute, and then treating the resulting protest as a policing problem. That lesson, learned from Ipperwash, is one that Canadian governments have been slow to absorb. What Came After, and What Hasn’t In December 2007, the Ontario government announced it would return Ipperwash Provincial Park to the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation. The formal settlement was completed on April 14, 2016, with a payment of $95 million. The park, with its long sandy beach on Lake Huron, is now Kettle and Stony Point territory. Camp Ipperwash, where the families have been living since 1993, is a different story. The federal government still controls the former military base. It is contaminated with unexploded ordnance, grenades, and artillery shells left over from decades of military training. As of the most recent reporting, decontamination is expected to take another 25 years. The families are living on land that the government is in the process of cleaning up. They are living, in other words, on a site that the federal government made dangerous, in order to reclaim land their families were removed from by force. The burial ground at the former park, whose presence the Stoney Point people had been trying to protect all along, was confirmed by archaeological survey in 2010. Fifteen years after Dudley George was shot for trying to protect it. Justice Linden’s policing recommendations were partially adopted. The OPP developed new protocols for Indigenous occupations, an approach focused on communication and patience rather than tactical escalation. Those protocols were put to a significant test at Caledonia in 2006, where a Six Nations land dispute stretched on for years with a notably different policing posture than Ipperwash. Whether that difference was due to Ipperwash’s lessons, or to the legal and political environment that had shifted around the duty to consult, is hard to separate. What has not changed is the underlying dynamic. Canada still has hundreds of unresolved land claims. Governments still routinely allow them to sit unaddressed for decades, and then express surprise when communities take direct action to assert what they believe is theirs. Grand Chief Joel Abram of the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians put it plainly in 2020: “The root of the problem is refusal to acknowledge Indigenous people’s rights to the land, and the colonialism that’s happened.” Thirty years later, that root has not been touched. The Pattern and the Present Ipperwash is an Ontario story, but its shape is recognizable from every other post in this series. A government takes land under pressure or emergency powers, with a promise to make it right later. Later never comes. The people whose land was taken exhaust every formal channel available to them. Then they act. And the state responds with force, or surveillance, or both, before ever seriously engaging with the underlying grievance. What changes over time is not the pattern but the legal framework around it. The Berger Inquiry in the 1970s built the case for environmental assessment and Indigenous participation in project reviews. Haida Nation in 2004 created a legally enforceable duty to consult before Crown decisions are made. Tsilhqot’in in 2014 confirmed that Aboriginal title is a real proprietary interest that the Crown must justify infringing. Each of these developments represents a narrowing of the space governments have to ignore Indigenous rights before those rights trigger legal obligations. Ipperwash did not produce a court decision. It produced an inquiry, and the inquiry produced recommendations, some of which were adopted. But the political dimension of what happened — a premier directing police to remove protesters from land the protesters had a legitimate claim to, based on a broken wartime promise — is not something any legal framework has yet fully addressed. The inquiry could name it. It could not remedy it. What does remedy look like? The George family would say it looks like the camp, fully decontaminated, fully returned, the promise finally kept. The Stoney Point people who have been living there since 1993, who refused to leave even as the army did, who are living now among the unexploded shells, might say the same thing. Dudley George died trying to make the government follow through on its word. That is not an act of extremism. It is what happens when a government breaks a promise, and then sends police to protect the broken promise from the people to whom it was made to. This is not only history. Proposed federal legislation is currently moving to streamline environmental assessments and reduce Indigenous consultation requirements for infrastructure projects, on the grounds that the process is too slow. The families of Aazhoodena waited fifty years. Their land still is not fully back. The land remembers who is still waiting. The people remember. Anthony “Dudley” George, 1957–1995. Aazhoodena. Welcome to Unceded Futures — Revised A note on this post: This is an updated version of the launch post from June 2025. The publication has now been running for nine months. This revision reflects more clearly what Unceded Futures is, who it’s for, and where I stand in relation to it. Who I Am and Why That Matters I am a settler. I was born and raised in Canada, I built a career in this country’s resource and infrastructure sector, and I have benefited from systems that were built, in part, on the dispossession of Indigenous peoples. That is not a confession. It is a starting point. For over twenty years I worked as an environmental consultant conducting impact assessments for resource projects across Canada. Mines, pipelines, transmission lines, dams. I reviewed plans, studied land, and engaged communities, both settler and Indigenous, in processes designed to evaluate whether a project should proceed and under what conditions. The longer I worked in that field, the harder it became to ignore a pattern. The projects got approved. The assessments got completed. The consultation boxes got checked. And the communities that had been living on and with that land for generations often ended up with less than they started with, or with promises that dissolved once the shovels were in the ground. I sold my consulting firm in 2024. Unceded Futures is what I started instead. What This Publication Is Unceded Futures examines infrastructure, land, and power. Each post focuses on a specific project, past or present, a railway, a pipeline, a dam, a military base, and asks the same set of questions: How did this get built? Who was on the land when it happened? Were they consulted, compensated, or simply removed? What did they do about it? And what are the legal and political consequences that are still playing out today? The posts are grounded in the legal arc of Indigenous rights in Canada, from the Calder decision in 1973, which first recognized Aboriginal title in Canadian law, through the Berger Inquiry, Sparrow, Delgamuukw, Haida Nation, Tsilhqot’in, and Yahey. Each of these cases moved the line on what governments are legally required to do before acting on Indigenous land. The posts trace that arc case by case, project by project, and show where the law has moved and where the gap between law and practice remains wide. This is not an Indigenous publication. I want to be clear about that. Unceded Futures does not speak for Indigenous communities or claim to represent their perspectives. It is a settler’s account of settler conduct, examined through the legal and historical record, with the aim of making that record harder to ignore. Why a Settler Should Write This It is a fair question. There are Indigenous writers, scholars, lawyers, and journalists doing this work with authority I don’t have. I read them and I recommend them and I will link to them wherever I can. What I can add is a specific vantage point: someone who spent two decades inside the environmental assessment process, who has sat in community consultation meetings and read the regulatory filings and watched the gap between the Crown’s stated commitments and its actual conduct. That experience does not make me an authority on Indigenous rights or Indigenous experience. It does make me a witness to how the system works, and to how often it doesn’t. The argument for writing this as a settler is simple. Reconciliation is not only Indigenous peoples’ work. The history of how this country was built is not only Indigenous peoples’ story to tell. Settlers have an obligation to understand it, to account for it, and to change the systems they operate in. This publication is my attempt to do that in the medium I know best. Why Now Two pieces of proposed legislation frame the present moment. Bill C-5 at the federal level and Bill 5 in Ontario are both aimed at accelerating infrastructure approvals by streamlining environmental assessments and reducing consultation requirements. The arguments for them are familiar: projects take too long, investment is being lost, Canada needs to move faster. The posts in this series are a response to that argument. Not by opposing infrastructure, but by asking what happens when governments have moved fast before, without consent, without adequate process, and without honouring their commitments. The answer is in the record. It is not reassuring. What’s Been Published Since June 2025, Unceded Futures has published six posts: The Canadian Pacific Railway and the dispossession of Indigenous peoples across the prairies and BC. The Canol Pipeline, built in 13 months on Sahtú Dene territory under the War Measures Act and abandoned, leaving a toxic legacy the community is still cleaning up. The Mackenzie Valley Pipeline inquiry, where Justice Thomas Berger spent three years listening to Dene and Métis and Gwich’in communities before recommending that no pipeline be built until land claims were settled. The James Bay hydroelectric project and the Cree and Inuit resistance that produced Canada’s first modern land claims agreement. The mercury poisoning at Grassy Narrows and the fifty-year fight for cleanup and accountability. And Ipperwash, where the Ontario government took land under wartime emergency powers, broke a fifty-year promise to return it, and then sent police when the families moved back. Each post is linked in the archive. If you’re new here, the Mackenzie Valley post is a good starting point. It’s the story of how environmental assessment in Canada was born, and what it was designed to prevent. What’s Coming The next posts will cover the Wet’suwet’en and the Coastal GasLink Pipeline, the Tsilhqot’in Nation and the Prosperity Mine, the Elsipogtog fracking blockade in New Brunswick, Site C, Lubicon Lake, and the Ring of Fire in northern Ontario. Each one follows the same structure: a specific project, a specific community, a specific legal and political turning point, and a bridge to the present. One post per month. Who This Is For Environmental assessment and resource industry practitioners who want to think more critically about the systems they work in. Students and educators in environmental studies, law, and Indigenous studies. Journalists and policy researchers. Community members and advocates seeking historical context and case law. And anyone who believes that future infrastructure in Canada should be built differently than it has been built before. If that’s you, subscribe. It’s free. It will stay free. Thanks for reading. In the early 1970s, Canada’s federal government was preparing to greenlight one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects in its history: a 1,200-kilometre natural gas pipeline that would snake through the Northwest Territories, following the Mackenzie River valley from the Beaufort Sea to Alberta. Backed by a powerful consortium of oil and gas companies, the Mackenzie Valley Pipeline was seen as a gateway to Arctic resource wealth and national energy security. But there was a problem, the land wasn’t empty. The Mackenzie Valley Pipeline promised energy and economic growth, but it also threatened the lands, waters, and lifeways of the Dene, Gwich’in, Métis, and Inuvialuit peoples who had lived there for millennia. Resistance from these Nations led to the Berger Inquiry, a groundbreaking public review that marked Canada’s first major environmental assessment process. But it was more than a bureaucratic milestone. For the first time, Indigenous voices were not only heard but central to decision-making. Their testimonies challenged assumptions about development, territory, and consent, setting a new precedent for how Canada engages with both the environment and the original stewards of the land. Echoes in the Tundra Every spring, the people watched the hills. They waited for the first dark line of caribou to crest the ridgeline, like beads moving across the land. Grandmothers boiled snow water in old kettles and told the children to listen; not with ears, but with the body. “You’ll feel them in your chest before you see them,” they’d say. “The land remembers their footsteps.” The caribou were not just animals. They were ancestors in another form, bringing meat, hide, and spirit. Their migration taught patience, taught movement, taught balance. And always, just as the caribou returned, the ice on the Mackenzie would break; slow at first, then all at once, the great river breathing again after a long sleep. But one year, something was different. The river groaned too early. Planes came. Roads followed. Survey lines cut across trails older than memory. In places where caribou once crossed in thousands, there were now fences of orange tape, thudding machines, and strangers taking core samples of the earth like it was theirs to dissect. Elders gathered and said, if the caribou stop coming, the land is trying to tell us something. Young people listened. Some left school to speak for the land. One of them was named Frank. He had watched the caribou every year of his life. When he stood to testify, he didn’t talk about politics or economics. He talked about water, about migration, about what happens when the river is strangled and the caribou turn away. Because when the caribou stop, it is not just their silence. It is a silence in the people, too. From Dene Resistance to a National Reckoning The Dene, Gwich’in, Métis, and Inuvialuit peoples had lived in the Mackenzie Valley for thousands of years. Their lives followed the migrations of caribou and the seasonal rhythms of rivers and ice. They had treaties, but no settled land claims. And crucially, they had not been asked. By 1974, the Dene Nation (then called the Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories) had become increasingly organized, politically active, and clear in their demands: no development without land rights and consent. They viewed the pipeline not just as a threat to the environment, but as part of a broader project of colonization; an attempt to permanently industrialize the North without Indigenous permission. At the time, Pierre Trudeau’s federal government was under pressure to balance economic expansion with rising social awareness, particularly around Indigenous rights. The 1969 White Paper, which had attempted to eliminate Indian status and “assimilate” Indigenous peoples, had already triggered a backlash and a rise in Indigenous political mobilization across the country. Amid growing resistance in the North, and an awareness that a major misstep could spark deeper conflict, the government made a surprising decision: to pause and listen. Enter Justice Thomas Berger In 1974, Justice Thomas Berger, a B.C. Supreme Court judge with a background in civil rights law and Indigenous justice, was appointed to lead a formal inquiry into the pipeline. The Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Inquiry, often simply called the Berger Inquiry, would become the first of its kind in Canada: a sweeping, multi-year public review of an energy megaproject that put environmental and Indigenous concerns at the centre. Berger didn’t just host hearings in Ottawa or Yellowknife. He traveled to 35 communities across the North, many only accessible by boat or plane, and held hearings in English, Dene, Gwich’in, Inuvialuktun and Métis languages. People spoke in gyms, church basements, and community halls. Over 1,000 individuals gave testimony, trappers, elders, youth, hunters, community leaders, many for the first time in a public forum. The Berger Inquiry was unlike anything Canada had seen. In town after town, Indigenous people stood before a government-appointed judge and flipped the power dynamic, using public testimony not only to voice opposition but to reassert sovereignty. They did not speak the language of policy and permits. They spoke of relationships; to land, to water, to ancestors, and of what would be lost if a pipeline cut through the heart of it all. The Testimonies That Changed Everything Among the most searing testimonies came from Chief Frank T’Seleie, then a 24-year-old leader from Fort Good Hope. In Fort Franklin (now Délı̨nę), standing before Justice Berger and representatives of powerful oil companies, he delivered a speech that would come to symbolize the Indigenous resistance of the era. He looked directly at the representatives of the oil companies and said: “You are committing genocide against us.” It was a shocking statement, not made lightly. T’Seleie went on to explain that while settlers had once used rifles and disease to displace Indigenous people, the pipeline was a new form of destruction: one cloaked in business suits, backed by money and machines. It would devastate the land and, with it, the people who depended on it for physical, cultural, and spiritual sustenance. He said: “You are talking about taking away from us the very things that keep us alive... We are not opposed to development. We are opposed to being destroyed by it.” T’Seleie’s message was not just resistance, it was vision. He didn’t call for isolation or denial of progress. He called for recognition, land rights, and a seat at the table. For the North to be developed, yes, but with Indigenous consent, control, and protection of traditional lifeways. A Gwich’in elder stated: “You talk about gas and oil. We talk about caribou and fish. When you hurt the water, you hurt us. What you call wilderness is our home.” A Métis hunter from Fort Simpson testified: “We don’t want to stop change. But we want to be alive to see it. Don’t ask us to trade our future for your fuel.” An Inuvialuit woman shared: “I speak for my grandchildren. If the land is gone, what stories will we tell them? What food will they eat?” Their messages echoed the same core truth: the land is not a resource, it is a relative. Berger’s Verdict These testimonies were not only persuasive, they were transformative. Berger later acknowledged that hearing from those most directly affected changed his own view of the project. In the end, he didn’t just deliver a technical report. He delivered a moral judgment. Justice Berger went far beyond analyzing economic feasibility or engineering challenges. His conclusion was rooted in a moral reckoning: that no project, no matter how profitable, should proceed if it threatens the survival, culture, and rights of the people who live on the land. He recognized that the pipeline posed irreversible risks not only to fragile northern ecosystems but to Indigenous nations whose voices had long been ignored in Canada's development agenda. “No pipeline should be built now through the Mackenzie Valley. We must first settle the land claims of the native people, and we must reach agreement with them on terms of development.” — Justice Thomas Berger, Final Report, 1977 Berger called for a 10-year moratorium not simply to delay construction, but to allow time for Indigenous land claims to be resolved and for Northern communities to shape their own future. His judgment reframed development as a question not of whether it can be done, but whether it should be, and who gets to decide. The Birth of Environmental Assessment in Canada Before the Berger Inquiry, there were no legal requirements in Canada to consider environmental impacts or consult the public, let alone Indigenous peoples, before launching massive industrial projects. Development decisions were made behind closed doors, driven largely by economic interests and federal priorities. The Mackenzie Valley Pipeline changed that. In appointing Justice Thomas Berger to lead the inquiry in 1974, the federal government was responding not just to local resistance but to a growing awareness across the country: Canada could no longer afford to ignore the environmental and social costs of development. The inquiry broke new ground by considering not just economic benefits, but cultural, ecological, and community well-being. Berger’s 1977 final report called for more than just a pause on the pipeline. It recommended permanent reforms: that any major development project in Canada should undergo a full environmental assessment, and that such assessments must include meaningful Indigenous and public participation. Berger’s 1977 final report laid the groundwork for Canada’s first formal environmental assessment process: the Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order (EARPGO, 1977). While EARPGO marked a critical turning point, its limitations eventually led to the creation of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act (CEAA) in 1992, later revised in 2012 to expand federal responsibilities. Most recently, Canada introduced the Impact Assessment Act (2019), which more explicitly embeds Indigenous rights, public participation, and sustainability into federal project reviews. Today, however, we face a new crossroads. Proposed legislation such as Bill C-5 at the federal level and Bill 5 in Ontario seeks to streamline environmental assessments by reducing what some view as regulatory “red tape.” Yet many fear that these changes could undermine decades of hard-won progress, weakening environmental oversight and eroding Indigenous engagement that began with Berger’s vision for just and inclusive development. Each of these steps traces its lineage back to Berger. When Listening Became Law The Berger Inquiry became a model for environmental review worldwide. It showed that development decisions could be paused, not to stop progress, but to make it more just, informed, and inclusive. And critically, it reframed Indigenous peoples not as “stakeholders,” but as rights-holders with inherent authority over their lands. It marked the moment when Canada began, haltingly, imperfectly, to recognize that environmental protection and Indigenous consent are not obstacles to development, but the foundation of sustainable futures. The Day the Strangers Came: A Cree Story of the First Hydro-Québec Arrival I remember it was late summer, the kind of day when the moss feels warm under your boots and the sound of geese fills the sky. We were in Waskaganish, the old people sitting by the fire, the young ones out setting snares or checking the water for fish. It had been quiet that season, no trouble, no big stories. Until the strangers came. They arrived by floatplane, their engines breaking the stillness of the bay. Some of the men had been out on the land when they spotted the planes circling low, making a racket over the rivers. Not many outsiders came up this way; we knew the Hudson’s Bay post, the missionaries, sure, but this was different. These ones didn’t come to trade or preach. They came with maps, blueprints, and the look of people who had already decided what was going to happen. They called themselves Hydro-Québec, some from the government too. They came ashore in shiny boots with rolled-up maps under their arms, telling us they were here to bring progress. They talked fast, in French and English, but not Cree. Their words didn’t sit right with us; they spoke of dams, roads, and power lines, like they already owned the rivers and the forests. I remember the look on the old hunters’ faces when they spread the maps on the table in the band office. Lines drawn over the land as if our rivers were theirs to move, our lakes theirs to flood. The La Grande, they said, was going to be turned into a mighty source of electricity, for the good of Quebec, for the good of everyone. But they weren’t talking about us. No one had come to ask permission. They hadn’t sat with the elders, shared tea, listened to the stories of the land. They hadn’t seen the traplines, the burial sites along the shores, the places where we taught our children to hunt and fish. They saw empty space on a map, but we saw home. At first, some thought maybe it was just more talk, but then the bulldozers came. Planes dropped supplies. Roads were cut through the forest without so much as a knock on the door. That’s when we understood this wasn’t just talk; they were already carving up Eeyou Istchee. The elders called meetings, the young people listened closely. We decided we couldn’t let them take the land without a fight. It wasn’t just about hunting or fishing, it was about survival. If the rivers changed, everything changed. The fish, the beavers, the birds, even the seasons themselves would be different. That was the beginning, the moment the outside world forced its way in. But it was also when we found our voice, when the people began to stand together. We didn’t have much in the way of lawyers or politicians back then, but we had the stories of our ancestors, the knowledge of the land, and the will to protect it. We didn’t ask for this fight, but we took it up all the same. The James Bay Hydroelectric Project: Quebec’s Northern Ambitions Long before the first dam was poured or heavy equipment carved roads into the forests of northern Quebec, government officials, engineers, and politicians were already looking north. As early as the 1950s, the province of Quebec had begun quietly exploring the vast hydroelectric potential of the James Bay region, a remote and largely untouched expanse of boreal forest, lakes, and powerful rivers stretching toward Hudson Bay. For Quebec, energy was more than just electricity. It was seen as a cornerstone of economic development and provincial identity. In the post-war years, the province was eager to modernize, industrialize, and, crucially, control its own resources. Northern Quebec, with its sprawling network of rivers, held the promise of exactly that. The La Grande, Eastmain, and Rupert rivers, among others, were singled out by engineers and planners for their enormous hydro potential. Their fast-flowing waters, steady year-round volume, and relative isolation made them prime candidates for large-scale dam construction and power generation. At the time, much of this interest unfolded behind government doors, in technical reports, and among a handful of powerful decision-makers. The people who lived along those rivers, the Cree and Inuit, whose families had hunted, fished, and trapped on the land for generations, were largely left out of the conversation. Their presence and rights were rarely, if ever, acknowledged in the early plans. By the end of the 1960s, as Hydro-Québec grew into one of the world’s largest public utilities and the idea of energy independence took hold in the province, those quiet studies and backroom conversations began to crystallize into formal proposals. What followed in the early 1970s would forever change the landscape of the North, spark one of the most significant Indigenous rights movements in Canadian history, and reshape the relationship between development and consent in the country. We Were Never Asked, But We Answered In 1971, Premier Robert Bourassa stood before Quebecers with what he described as the key to the province’s future. His government announced the James Bay Hydroelectric Project, a massive $6 billion development plan that would tap into the rivers of the North to generate electricity on an unprecedented scale. For Bourassa, it was more than a construction project. It was the foundation for economic independence, job creation, and energy security in Quebec. He famously declared it would be the “project of the century.” At the heart of the plan was the La Grande River basin, a vast network of waterways flowing west toward James Bay. The project called for the construction of a series of dams, reservoirs, and generating stations that would drastically reshape the region. Entire river systems would be diverted, vast areas of land would be flooded, and new roads and transmission lines would cut through some of the most remote territory in Canada. The project was to be managed by Hydro-Québec, the province’s public utility, working through a new government agency known as the James Bay Development Corporation, or in French, the Société de développement de la Baie James. Construction was set to begin quickly, with little consideration for the people who lived on the land. For the Cree and Inuit of northern Quebec, this announcement was not an exciting promise of progress. It was a direct threat to their way of life. The project would flood hunting grounds, disrupt fish and wildlife populations, and bring roads and machinery into regions that had remained largely untouched. Most importantly, the decision had been made without their knowledge, consultation, or consent. By 1972, Cree leaders established the Grand Council of the Crees, and the Inuit formed the Northern Quebec Inuit Association. These new political organizations gave their communities a united voice, determined to fight back against the project that threatened their land, their hunting grounds, and their way of life. “We were never asked. The government had already made up its mind,” recalled Billy Diamond, the young Cree leader from Waskaganish who became Grand Chief at just 21. “They saw the land as empty. But for us, this is home.” The Cree and Inuit quickly realized that legal action was their most immediate tool. Their lawyers filed for an injunction in Quebec Superior Court, arguing that the project violated their rights. It was a bold move for small, remote communities facing the full weight of the Quebec government and Hydro-Québec. “We were told that development was inevitable,” said Philip Awashish, a Cree negotiator from Mistissini. “But we also knew that we had rights, even if the government didn’t recognize them yet. We had to test that in court.” In the fall of 1973, their case landed before Justice Albert Malouf. For weeks, Cree and Inuit witnesses, elders, and legal experts presented evidence of their relationship to the land, their dependence on the rivers and wildlife, and the devastating impact the project would bring. On November 15, 1973, Justice Malouf delivered his decision. It was a shock to many. He ruled that construction on the James Bay Project must stop, citing the serious and irreparable harm it posed to the Cree and Inuit and recognizing that their rights had not been extinguished. “We were relieved, but also cautious,” remembered Charlie Watt, one of the Inuit negotiators. “The decision was a victory, but we knew the fight wasn’t over.” In fact, the Malouf injunction was quickly overturned on appeal, and construction resumed. But the legal and political pressure created by the resistance could not be ignored. The decision had forced governments and Hydro-Québec to the negotiating table, setting the stage for the first modern Indigenous land claims agreement in Canada. For the Cree and Inuit, the message was clear. As Billy Diamond would later say, “We may be small in number, but when we stand together, we are not powerless.” A New Kind of Agreement: Negotiating the James Bay and Northern Quebec Settlement The legal battle may not have stopped the bulldozers for long, but it sent a clear message: development in the North could not continue as if the Cree and Inuit were invisible. The court case had cracked open the door, and Cree and Inuit leaders intended to keep pushing. Throughout 1973 and 1974, political pressure mounted. International media began paying attention, exposing how Quebec’s grand plans for energy expansion came at the expense of Indigenous rights and the environment. The Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in the Calder case, which confirmed that Aboriginal title existed in Canadian law, only strengthened the Cree and Inuit position. They now had legal precedent on their side. Quebec and Canada, recognizing the risk of prolonged legal uncertainty and public controversy, agreed to sit down with Indigenous leaders to negotiate a formal settlement. These were not easy talks. The relationship between the Cree and Inuit and the provincial government had been badly strained by years of exclusion and disregard. But both sides understood that a different approach was needed. The negotiations that followed were groundbreaking in Canadian history. Rather than settling for compensation alone, Cree and Inuit leaders demanded a comprehensive agreement that would recognize their rights, protect their way of life, and provide a real voice in the development of their homeland. In November 1975, after months of tense discussions, the parties signed the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement (JBNQA). It was the first modern land claims settlement in Canada, often described as the country’s first “modern treaty.” The agreement recognized Cree and Inuit rights to land, hunting, and resource use. It also provided financial compensation, along with guarantees for education, health services, and local governance. Importantly, the agreement created a new framework for how development would proceed in the region. It required consultation, environmental and social protections, and the establishment of joint management boards where Cree and Inuit representatives would have a seat at the table. While not perfect, the JBNQA marked a turning point. It showed that Indigenous peoples could no longer be sidelined in the decisions that shaped their lands and futures. It was a turning point that would echo far beyond the rivers of northern Quebec, influencing policies, courtrooms, and resource projects across the country. For the Cree and Inuit, the agreement was both a compromise and a hard-won recognition. The hydro project would proceed, but so would their political and legal presence. The days of ignoring northern communities were over, at least in principle. The struggle had forced a new conversation about development, consent, and the meaning of rights in Canada. A New Era for Resource Development and Environmental Law The James Bay Project changed the rules for resource development across Canada. For the Cree and Inuit, it marked a turning point in their fight for rights and recognition. For governments, industries, and the courts, it exposed a new reality: Indigenous peoples could no longer be excluded from the decisions shaping their homelands. The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement was the first formal recognition that Indigenous peoples could not be sidelined from decisions that reshaped their territories. Though the project moved ahead, it did so with the Cree and Inuit at the table, negotiating terms, protections, and long-term benefits. It was an imperfect victory, but it set a precedent that has echoed through every major project since. “Before James Bay, development just happened to us,” Cree leader Philip Awashish later reflected. “After James Bay, we had a voice, and we had rights that governments could no longer ignore.” The Roots of Environmental Assessment in Canada The project also exposed a glaring gap in Canadian law: the absence of a structured process to assess and regulate the environmental and social impacts of development. At the time, there was no formal environmental assessment (EA) regime in place. The Malouf decision and the public outcry over James Bay helped force that conversation to the forefront. By the late 1970s and early 1980s, Canada began building its first generation of environmental assessment policies and legislation, aimed at preventing the kind of exclusion and environmental risks seen in James Bay. Provinces developed their own EA regimes, and at the federal level, processes evolved that would eventually lead to the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act of 1992, and later, its modern successor, the Impact Assessment Act. Critically, these processes began to embed the principle that Indigenous peoples must be consulted on projects affecting their territories. Over time, this evolved into the legal duty to consult and accommodate, now a cornerstone of resource development in Canada. A Legacy of Inclusion and Unfinished Work The James Bay conflict also shifted public expectations. Environmental groups, legal scholars, and Indigenous organizations increasingly demanded that development could not come at the expense of rights, cultures, or ecosystems. The project sparked decades of legal and political change that continue to shape Canada’s approach to energy, mining, and infrastructure development today. For the Cree and Inuit, the James Bay experience was both a loss and a victory. The rivers were diverted, but their rights were recognized. The land was altered, but their place at the decision-making table was secured. The so-called project of the century may have begun without them, but it ensured that no future development in Canada would happen without their voice. Thanks for reading!
